prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Connect 4 game on a 6x7 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board: list[list[int]]) -> int: ... ``` # State Representation - The board is a 6x7 grid. - You are always the current player when `policy` is called. - `board` is a 6x7 grid of ints with the following encoding: - `0` represents an empty cell. - `1` represents your disc (current player). - `-1` represents the opponent's disc. - Rows are indexed from `0` (top) to `5` (bottom). - Columns are indexed from `0` to `6`. - When a disc is dropped into a column, it occupies the lowest available empty cell in that column. # Action / Return Format - Return an integer column index `col` in the range `0-6`. - The chosen column must not be full (i.e., it must contain at least one `0`). - Your disc will be placed in the lowest available row in that column. - The objective is to form a horizontal, vertical, or diagonal line of four of your discs. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning to build a Connect 4 AI using minimax with alpha-beta pruning and bitboards for efficient board representation, where each column uses 7 bits to encode piece positions across the 6 rows.

Now I'm working through the bitboard conversion logic—scanning each column from bottom to top to map the board state into bit positions, then implementing win detection by checking for four consecutive pieces in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal directions using bit shifts.

Implementing win detection... I'm settling on a simpler heuristic based on center preference and threat counting, then using iterative deepening with a time limit to search as deep as possible within about 0.85 seconds. I'm building out the full policy function that parses the board into bitboards, tracks column heights, and runs the negamax search with alpha-beta pruning.

Implementing win detection and search logic... Precomputing all 69 possible 4-in-a-row windows as bitmasks...

Now I'm building the heuristic function that scores positions by counting my pieces and opponent pieces in each window, assigning points for threats and blocking opportunities...

The performance is acceptable at 69 iterations per call, so I'll keep this approach. For the negamax algorithm, I'm setting up the core minimax search with alpha-beta pruning, checking for immediate winning moves first using a center-biased column order, then recursively evaluating opponent responses while tracking time to avoid timeout...

Generating the precomputed windows... Continuing the negamax search logic, I'm iterating through possible moves, recursively evaluating positions with alpha-beta pruning to find the best column to play. Then in the policy function, I'm parsing the board state into bitboards and heights, checking for immediate wins or forced blocks before launching into the full negamax search with a time deadline.

Now I'm realizing there's a subtle bug: when negamax checks if the current player can win immediately, after the opponent moves, the roles flip—what was the opponent's board becomes the new "my" board in the recursive call, so I need to make sure the win condition is being evaluated correctly from the right perspective. When I place a piece, negamax will explore the opponent's response and catch any winning moves they have available, so that's handled implicitly. For efficiency, I should implement iterative deepening that only saves results after completing a full depth search, so if a timeout occurs mid-search, I fall back to the last fully-explored depth rather than a partial result. Verifying the bitboard layout and shift operations for win detection—each column uses 7 bits with the sentinel row preventing vertical wraparound, and the shift amounts (1 for vertical, 7 for horizontal, 6 and 8 for diagonals) correctly map to adjacent positions without crossing column boundaries.

Now I'm concerned about performance since popcount gets called on 69 windows at every leaf node, so I'll use Python's built-in `bit_count()` method when available, falling back to `bin(x).count('1')` for compatibility.

Generating the window bitmasks... Implementing the game tree search with alpha-beta pruning to evaluate moves, then checking for immediate wins before falling back to blocking opponent threats or exploring deeper positions. I'm verifying the board parsing logic handles the piece placement correctly by checking from the bottom up, and everything looks good. I think this solution is ready to go.
